title: Print Statements
summary: Write text to the console with System.out.println and print, escape sequences, and text blocks.
intro: Every program talks to you through its output. In Java that starts with `System.out.println`, inside a `Main` class.

steps.title: println and print

example.title: Welcome banner
example.prompt: Print a three-line welcome banner, an empty line, and a lesson line built from print and println.
example.output:
Welcome to Hack University
Learn Java one step at a time
Let's write some code!

Lesson 1: print
example.explanation: Each `println` prints its text and ends the line. The empty `println()` makes the blank line. `print("Lesson 1: ")` leaves the cursor at the end of that text, so `println("print")` continues on the same line and then ends it. The `//` lines are comments and print nothing.

practice.title: Course card
practice.prompt:
Print a course card, an empty line, and a progress line.

1. Print `Course: Data Structures`, `Level: Beginner`, and `Status: Enrolled` on three lines with `println`.
2. Print an empty line with `System.out.println()`.
3. Print `Progress: ` with one `print` call, then finish the line with `println("0%")`.

Expected output:

```text
Course: Data Structures
Level: Beginner
Status: Enrolled

Progress: 0%
```

tests.output:
Course: Data Structures
Level: Beginner
Status: Enrolled

Progress: 0%

hints: Use one `System.out.println` per card line, and end each statement with `;`.
`System.out.println()` with nothing inside prints the empty line.
`System.out.print("Progress: ")` stays on the line, so the next `println` finishes it.

steps.title: Escape sequences
steps.body:
Some characters cannot be typed straight into a string. A backslash starts an **escape sequence**, which stands for one special character:

| Escape | Prints |
| --- | --- |
| `\n` | a new line |
| `\t` | a tab |
| `\"` | a double quote |
| `\\` | one backslash |

```java
System.out.println("Line one\nLine two");
System.out.println("Name\tAge");
System.out.println("She said \"hi\"");
System.out.println("C:\\temp");
```

`\n` lets one `println` print several lines. A tab jumps to the next tab stop, which lines up short columns. Checkers compare the tab character itself, so spaces that look the same do not match.

The classic gotcha is a Windows path. `"C:\temp"` compiles, but `\t` becomes a tab and prints `C:` then a gap then `emp`. Always double the backslash. An unknown escape is worse: `"C:\Users"` does not compile at all, because `\U` is not an escape.

example.title: Cafe receipt
example.prompt: Print a two-row receipt with tab-separated columns, a line with a quoted name, and a folder path.
example.output:
Tea	2.50
Cake	4.00
Today's special: "Lemon Tart"
Receipt saved to C:\temp
example.explanation: In the first `println`, each `\t` becomes a tab and the `\n` starts a new line, so one call prints both rows. `\"` puts a double quote inside the string without ending it. `\\` prints a single backslash, so the path comes out as `C:\temp` instead of `C:` plus a tab.

practice.title: File report
practice.prompt:
Print a file name in quotes, its Windows path, and a two-row score table.

1. Print `File: "notes.txt"` with the quotes, using `\"`.
2. Print `Path: C:\Users\ada\notes.txt`, writing each backslash as `\\`.
3. Print the table with one `println`: separate the columns with `\t` and the two rows with `\n`.

Expected output:

```text
File: "notes.txt"
Path: C:\Users\ada\notes.txt
Ada	95
Lin	88
```
hints: Inside a string, `\"` prints `"` and `\\` prints one backslash.
Put a `\t` between each name and its score, and a `\n` between the two rows, all in one string.

steps.title: Text blocks (Java 15)
steps.body:
A **text block** (Java 15) is a multi-line string between triple quotes. You write the lines as they should look, with no `\n` escapes for new lines and no `\"` escapes for quotes.

```java
System.out.print("""
    Hello
      indented
    World
    """);
```

The rules:

- The content starts on the line after the opening `"""`. Text on that same line is a compile error.
- Java removes the smallest indentation shared by the content lines and the closing `"""` line. Extra indentation beyond that is kept, so `indented` keeps its two spaces.
- Trailing spaces at the end of each line are removed.
- With the closing `"""` on its own line, the text ends with a newline. Print it with `print`, because `println` would add an empty line.
- Escapes still work. Write a backslash as `\\`.

Gotcha: moving the closing `"""` further left than the content makes it the smallest indentation, so every line gains extra leading spaces.

example.title: House banner
example.prompt: Print a small boxed banner with a roof from one text block.
example.explanation: The box lines and the closing `"""` all start 12 spaces in, so Java removes 12 spaces from every line. The roof lines start 2 and 1 spaces further in, so they keep that extra indentation. Each `\\` prints one backslash. The block ends with a newline, so `print` adds nothing more.

practice.title: Menu board
practice.prompt:
Print a four-line menu board from one text block.

1. Call `System.out.print` with one text block.
2. Indent the price line two spaces more than the other lines.
3. Write the bowl `\_/` on the last line as `\\_/`.

Expected output:

```text
TODAY'S MENU
Tomato Soup
  Price: $4
\_/ Enjoy!
```

tests.output:
TODAY'S MENU
Tomato Soup
  Price: $4
\_/ Enjoy!

hints: Start with `System.out.print("""`, put the lines below it, and close with `""");` on its own line.
Line the closing `"""` up with the menu lines so their indentation is removed, and give the price line two extra spaces.
A backslash inside a text block is still written `\\`.

recap:
- `System.out.println("text")` prints a line, `System.out.print` stays on the line, and `System.out.println()` prints an empty line.
- Every statement ends with `;` and `//` starts a comment.
- `\n` new line, `\t` tab, `\"` quote, `\\` backslash. Double every backslash in a path.
- A text block starts on the line after `"""`, loses its shared indentation and trailing spaces, and ends with a newline when the closing `"""` sits on its own line, so print it with `print`.
